title: The 10 Best Zigbee Hubs and Coordinators
subtitle: Zigbee USB coordinators and standalone hubs, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: We pulled the Zigbee coordinators and hubs selling on Amazon and scored them on rating, review volume, and features: open Zigbee 3.0 pairing, Thread support on the same radio, and network (Ethernet or PoE) connections. The table shows whether each is a stick or a hub.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

avoid.name: Tuya Smart Multi-Mode Gateway, Zigbee 3.0, BLE, Bluetooth Mesh, Smart Home Wireless Hub for Home Automation, Wifi 2.4G/5G Dual-band, APP Control, Voice Control, Compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant
avoid.verdict: The listing contradicts itself: it says there's "no fear of disconnecting from the Ethernet" on a Wi-Fi gateway with no Ethernet port listed, and it sends device data to the cloud.
reasons: It mentions Ethernet, but connection is described only as 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi and the box contents list a USB power cable, no Ethernet.
It says its USB-C power complies with "the latest EU regulations" on a US listing.
It claims Siri support but lists no HomeKit or Matter support to back that up.
Device signals are uploaded to the cloud server, per the listing, so control depends on Tuya's cloud.

buyers_guide.a: A USB stick (or network coordinator) is just a radio. It needs software running on something else, usually Home Assistant on a mini PC or a Home Assistant Green. A full hub has the radio and the automation software in one box, so it works out of the box but you're tied to its app.

buyers_guide.q: Can I move my devices to a new hub later?
buyers_guide.a: Usually not without re-pairing each device. Z-Wave controllers can sometimes back up and restore their network, and some Zigbee coordinators can be migrated in Home Assistant, but plan on re-pairing if you switch brands.

Somewhere central and out in the open, not in a metal cabinet or right next to the router. For USB sticks, use a short USB extension cable to move the stick away from the computer, since USB 3 ports put out interference that hurts 2.4 GHz radios.
